symptom.title: Excessive verification
symptom.summary: An agent continues or expands verification beyond the task’s justified checking needs, delaying the requested outcome.

observation.p: The agent spends effort checking things that do not help the user’s actual goal, planned review, or credible failure risks, delaying useful work or adding avoidable cost. This can happen on the first check: no repeated run or explicit time limit is required.

The agent verifies at a level suited to a different task: it hardens a disposable prototype when the user wants feedback, takes over review the user intends to do, or tests states the application cannot reach.

how-to-recognize-it.p: Read the user’s request and follow-up messages beside the checks the agent performed: what was the user trying to learn, what would they review themselves, and what could actually fail? A human or classifier can identify a mismatch without a predeclared time budget.

lookalike.p: The user wants a release, or the change could cause a consequential failure. Checking that risk serves the task even when it takes longer than the edit; a rule’s mere existence does not establish that it is appropriate.

The user wants help with verification, or the agreed workflow assigns those checks to the agent. This differs from assuming the agent must do every check when the user has chosen to handle part of the review.
A new failure or a real interaction in the application justifies a broader check. The agent should be able to name that risk; the number of tests alone does not show excess.
The user is investigating flakiness or reliability. Repeated runs answer the question they asked, even when the code is unchanged.

what-to-record.p: Keep the user’s goal, intended review, urgency, and relevant instructions alongside the checks performed. Describe why each disputed check did or did not help, including what could actually fail in the application. Record delay, cost, useful defects found, and the user’s corrections where available; exact timing or a predeclared budget is helpful but not required.

example.p: A founder asks for a clickable mockup to show five prospective customers that afternoon. The agent spends forty minutes adding file-integrity checks to static demo assets. The request and command log make the mismatch visible: the checks do not help learn whether customers want the idea, and the feedback session starts without the mockup.

A user asks for a small UI change and says they will check the visual result themselves. The agent spends another twenty minutes building screenshot comparisons before showing the page. It has taken over review the user chose to do and delayed that review.

The application creates a fixed internal list; users cannot change its shape. After a label edit, the agent writes a suite for malformed external versions of that list. Reading where the list is constructed shows those inputs cannot reach this code, and the tests delay the requested change without covering a real risk.

A developer describes a week of expanding reviews and more than 4,000 tests, ending with CI blocked. The author later clarified that features did exist, but described the testing as mismatched to an early product. This is a report of workflow cost and unmet intent, not proof that every test was unnecessary.

A Claude Code user reports repeated runs of more than 1,500 tests after small edits despite instructions to stop, estimating about two hours per run. This illustrates repeated checking; it is only one form of the symptom, and the report does not establish the need for each test.

A one-line authentication change takes one minute and its regression suite takes twelve. The suite checks a real access-control risk before a release the user requested. The longer check serves the task.
